name: Rhesus Isoimmunisation
aliases: haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

clinicalPearls: Rhesus isoimmunisation occurs when a Rh(D)-negative mother is exposed to Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells and develops anti-D antibodies that can cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies
Sensitising events include delivery, miscarriage, termination, ectopic pregnancy, antepartum bleeding, abdominal trauma, and invasive procedures such as amniocentesis
Because sensitisation usually produces no maternal symptoms, prevention and surveillance depend on routine antenatal blood grouping and antibody screening
Prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin given after sensitising events and routinely in the third trimester has dramatically reduced the incidence of the disease
Once a woman is sensitised, anti-D immunoglobulin is no longer protective, and management focuses on monitoring the fetus for anaemia
Fetal anaemia is assessed non-invasively by Doppler measurement of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, which rises as anaemia develops
Severe fetal anaemia can be treated by intrauterine transfusion, and timing of delivery is balanced against the severity of disease
Other red cell antibodies such as anti-Kell and anti-c can also cause severe haemolytic disease, so screening is not limited to the D antigen
reference.pathophysiology: When Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells enter the circulation of a Rh(D)-negative mother, her immune system mounts an antibody response, initially IgM and then IgG anti-D. In a later pregnancy with a Rh(D)-positive fetus, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, binds fetal red cells, and leads to their destruction in the fetal reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia drives extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, high-output cardiac failure with generalised oedema known as hydrops fetalis, alongside accumulation of bilirubin that threatens the neonate after birth.
additionalDifferentials: Haemolytic disease from non-D red cell antibodies such as anti-Kell or anti-c
Fetal anaemia from parvovirus B19 infection
Non-immune hydrops fetalis from cardiac or structural causes
additionalInvestigations: Maternal blood group and antibody screen at booking and repeated during pregnancy
Quantification and titre of anti-D and other clinically significant antibodies
Paternal and, where available, fetal Rh(D) genotyping including cell-free fetal DNA testing
Serial middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity to detect fetal anaemia
Ultrasound assessment for signs of hydrops
Kleihauer or flow cytometry to estimate the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage
redFlags: Rising antibody titres or Doppler velocities indicating progressive fetal anaemia and risk of fetal compromise
Ultrasound evidence of hydrops fetalis signalling severe disease
A significant sensitising event without timely anti-D prophylaxis
Reduced fetal movements or non-reassuring fetal assessment in a sensitised pregnancy
Previous pregnancy affected by severe haemolytic disease, predicting earlier and more severe recurrence
reference.prognosis: With routine antenatal screening, effective anti-D prophylaxis, non-invasive monitoring, and intrauterine transfusion, most affected pregnancies now achieve good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with early-onset severe anaemia and hydrops, and sensitised pregnancies tend to be affected earlier and more severely in successive gestations, making specialist surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Omitting anti-D prophylaxis after a sensitising event or assuming it helps an already sensitised woman
Focusing only on anti-D and overlooking other antibodies such as anti-Kell
Relying on antibody titres alone without fetal Doppler surveillance in established sensitisation
Underestimating small but sensitising fetomaternal haemorrhages
Failing to quantify large fetomaternal haemorrhage so that the anti-D dose is inadequate
management: Prevent sensitisation with prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin given routinely in the third trimester and after any sensitising event in Rh(D)-negative women
Determine foetal Rh(D) status by cell-free foetal DNA testing to identify pregnancies at risk
In sensitised pregnancies, monitor for foetal anaemia with serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler and ultrasound for hydrops
Perform intrauterine intravascular foetal transfusion for significant foetal anaemia
Time delivery and prepare neonatal care, treating haemolytic jaundice with phototherapy and exchange transfusion as required
Coordinate care in a foetal medicine unit with serial maternal antibody titres
